en: When the Blessed One is turned away from bestowing grace, even if one has set out upon that difficult-to-traverse path, the atom—standing in the state of perversion—never attains anything at all, however stable it may be within its five-fold stages. 100.

Even a man who has attained the circle of reality through great effort, yet remains outside the nectar of your scripture—despite the density of the expansion of the primordial nature and so forth—falls into the extreme of following the doctrines of the fettered. (101)

Those others, whose dense thickets of delusion remain unbroken, being defiled in soul and possessing only the lamp of the Paśupata doctrine, have undoubtedly become filled with darkness itself due to their failure to comprehend your scripture, even though they possess the excellence of atoms. 102.
O Lord of the Thirty-three, primordial nature (prakṛti) is not conscious of anything at all, and the person (puruṣa) is likewise indifferent;
yet it is you alone who, through your grace, manifest the activity of consciousness and truly bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 103.

Even though they remain non-different from the Supreme Person due to their mockery of a mere semblance of the equality of Dharma, others who are excluded from the nectar of your scripture consider themselves accomplished; yet they are unable to discern the difference between them. 104.
Indeed, the collection of words is twofold: that which loudly proclaims the teachings of Śiva and that which proclaims other doctrines.
O Bhava, the latter attains the state of being the sole cause for the higher and lower fruits of the world, while the former has you as its guide. 105.

O Lord of Mura, this fourfold consciousness, which resembles the natural luminosity of Hari, the firefly, the moon, and the sun, proceeds here, possessing degrees of excellence bestowed by Your grace. (106)
Through the path of yoga, one clearly attains freedom from doubt by means of the unerring scripture;
thus, O Ārivaṃsa, there are no discerning ones here who, having conquered the qualities of existence, continue to undergo the cycle of birth and death. 107.

Seated upon the throne of the sky, having dispelled all darkness and established your abode, you, desiring to manifest your entire sovereign majesty, have become gracious through the stainless rays of your own powers; thus, you have revealed the true nature of the aggregate of atoms.

O Lord of the Gods, by bestowing your grace upon this circle of limited souls, you cause their own selves to attain a state equal to yours—possessing the power of consciousness through the cognition of all objects without distinction, and possessing agency through the manifestation of the forms of all things. (109)

O Lord, that which indeed issued forth in the past from Your imperishable self, which is both being and non-being, in the form of sound—that flawless scripture, Sadāśiva, bearing it, then understood the entire reality of its meaning as resting upon that [sound]. 110.

Then Giriśa, with his four faces, gradually spoke that wonderful discourse, which contained the vast extent of the reality established in the eternal tradition of the infinite-faced Rudra-maṇḍala, and which was a dense thicket of mantras of many varieties. 111.

O Lord, from your mouth there has emerged here this lotus of the scriptures, which is fully blossomed with a mass of filaments that are the [eighteen] great topics (*guṇakesarotkara*), possessing a pure essence as its clearly manifest stalk (*dharmanāla*), raining down honey, and having the six categories of meaning (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) as its clearly visible bees. 112.

Having attained their own power to express every object, and having reached a state where the entire range of speech is contained within them as if they were the universal form itself—strung together with syllables that function with specific modifications conjoined by auxiliary factors—[they pervade] the world. (113)

Your power, O Mother, who originates from Your mouth, is indeed the *mātṛkā*, whose body consists of the eightfold classes of phonemes clearly manifest as the nature of the mantras and mandalas that bring success to the practitioner; she is established in the state of the reality of the three divisions. O Bhava, the forms of the mantras are composed of the letters of the *mātṛkā* that have emerged from Your mouth.
Having attained a state of detachment for the sake of liberation, those whose conduct is contrary [to this] instead bestow the enjoyments of worldly existence. // 115 //

O Blessed One, for those desiring to ascend to the eternal, upward-turning state, the entire path of all things is a ladder; yet, O Yogin, it is by You alone that this support, fixed upon the wall of Your own power, is provided as an intermediary. 116.

O Blessed One, even though You possess a form that is but a hundred-millionth part of a child, and although You have adopted a path characterized by the sixfold adjuncts—standing as a single entity, You cause wonder to arise in whose mind? Ah! You do so.

O Lord, we have heard that it was indeed Ananta, as you have clearly described, who first agitated the cave of the qualities (guṇaguhā); from that beginning, he created the world, both white and black, ending with the earth. 118.
Ananta, the sovereign of all Rudras, being impelled by you alone,
first agitated Māyā, which consists of the three qualities such as Sattva. Thereafter, beginning from that,
the world— including the principle of Māyā and the rest— arose, white and endowed with the quality of Sattva, as well as composed of Rajas and Tamas.
We, who have heard the sacred traditions (*āgama*), have heard that he created [the world] as far as the earth.
And it is said, beginning with the statement: "Māyā, though itself unshakeable, shakes Prakṛti," and so forth: "Taste shakes water, and smell..."
From "pṛthivīm" up to "tataḥ," [this constitutes] verse 118.

O Lord of the Gods, those very Śiva-śaktis, whose essence is identical with You, perform their respective functions in the world in succession; by means of them alone, You, the leader of all mantras, have by Your will manifested this entire universe. 119.
The powers of Śiva, such as Vāmā and the others, are deities; they perform actions that are of His very nature.
By means of those very actions, which serve as instruments, the leader of mantras named Ananta has created this world through Your will.
And it is said: "Endowed with the power and activity of Śiva, Ananta, the sovereign lord of all mantras, creates the entire world as impelled by the Blessed One. (119)

O Lord, the leaders of mantra do not indeed waver from their role in performing the preservation of the world’s stability and other such functions, even as they have entered into a state of cessation and dependence upon the will of others for the sake of the world. 120.

The leaders of the mantras, such as Ananteśa and others, do not deviate from the maintenance of the world’s established order and its boundaries solely through Your will; indeed, impelled by You alone,
they become the causes for protection and other such functions.
Cessation is the state of being incapable of acting due to the loss of power. // 120 //
O Lord of the Gods, the sovereigns of the deities beginning with Kamalāsana, together with their retinues, as described by you,
have become respectively the causes of the arising, the maintenance, and the dissolution of the succession of worlds in their threefold states.

And in due order, the lords of the gods beginning with Kamalāsana— namely Brahmā, Acyuta, and Hara— are, by virtue of being composed of the three aforementioned elements or of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, the causes of the birth and other states of the threefold world-system, yet they act only when impelled by You.
Those possessing *saṅga* (attachment) are impure in comparison to you, because they possess the nature of cattle (*paśu*). And it has been said:
"Even the lords of the gods, beginning with Brahmā, possess *saṅga*; impelled by that Great Lord (*Maheśvara*), they become the causes of the birth and so forth of the world. (121)
O Lord of the Gods, those renowned ones— Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya— who have attained the state of being Your forms,
from them indeed was she born here in this sequence of purification, endowed with the exquisite beauty of every limb.
The triad. // 122 //
To those who have attained the state of your eightfold form— Fire, Wind, and the Sun— from them [proceed]: "Phonetics, Ritual, Grammar, Astronomy, Prosody,
and Etymology."
Thus, the Triad—characterized by the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman*—together with the excellence of the six ancillary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), arose and became manifest in due order. And it has been said:
"Agni, Vāyu..."
O Giver of Boons, by Your will, the universal monarchs dwelling within various instruments abide in happiness,
taking refuge in diverse worlds contained within the interior of the manifest cave that grants all desires.
O Lord, agency can never be established even by the oaths uttered by others for those things whose nature consists of atoms and karma, which are insentient and devoid of any presiding self. // 125 //

With the state of consciousness stirred by a *kalā*, and perceiving objects through *vidyā*, this individual soul (*aṇu*), its mind dyed with firm passion, becomes a partaker of the experiences of *prakṛti* by the will of Bhava. (126)

Having drawn forth the multitudes of persons who are stained by the threefold impurity of the sheaths and who fall into the deep caverns of worldly enjoyment, you lead them far toward purity from the interior of the cave, according to your will. 127.
You do not release those helpless creatures who, longing for the circle of grass that is the realm of the mind, have long remained with their faces cast down,
their multitudes of bonds shattered by your compassion.
Of the fivefold nature. //128//
The sense is: "Whom would you not fill with wonder, standing as you do after having released the multitude of bonds that bind transmigrating beings (*paśu*)? ...
Desiring a circle of young grass with their faces turned downward, they have been freed from their ropes by someone."
"They are liberated only through [the Lord's] grace; and being embraced by necessity (niyati)—thus is the bound soul (paśu) said to possess five attributes. // 128 //
The power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*), whose operation is unimpeded and which consists of the atomic impurity (*āṇava-mala*), awakens to the reality residing within the objects of experience;
yet it is Your power, possessing a wondrous state that has attained a dual nature, that awakens that [atomic power] in its entirety. 129.
This power of consciousness belonging to the atomic souls (jīvas) is of two kinds, distinguished by pleasure and pain. An object existing within the range of the sense organs, such as the eye,
perceives that very thing as "existent" and cognizes it as "existent," because it does not cognize that which is separated by space and other such factors.

Your own consciousness-power (citiśakti), which is of two kinds— the differentiated (sakalā) enveloped by the principle of Kalā as the means for achieving both heaven and liberation, and the undifferentiated (niṣkalā)— awakens that [limited soul] with its unimpeded activity.
It renders one capable of perceiving objects that are obstructed. // 129 //
O Lord, even though this person is established within the path and is subtle, he is nonetheless bound by the form of a firm fetter;
yet, O Master, he is capable of experiencing that which lies beyond the sphere of his own self through Your power of *kalā*.
He was appointed. 130.

Even though the subtle *puruṣa* exists pervading the sixfold path beginning with *tattva* according to the *paddhati*, it is not capable of experiencing anything other than its own object, because it is constrained by the power of *kalā*. // 130 //

That illusion of yours, which reveals the state where ultimate reality has been removed while simultaneously concealing its very manifestation— by that illusion you are not mocked, for you are one whose bondage to existence has ceased.
The mind. 131.

He whose mind is bound by the attachment to the nature of objects within your domain, and who is fixed in devotion, is not mocked nor overcome by that *māyā*. To the question "By what [māyā]? he says:
by that which, having removed the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), establishes the existence of a phenomenon (*bhāva*) based on conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).

It manifests a state as if it were real; and it veils a thing that is actually real and manifesting, making it appear in another form, because its nature is delusive. Thus, [delusion] is cast off and rejected. 131.
O Bhava, while your body is being consecrated by the waters of the immortal river of pleasant sensations according to your will,
the impurities inherent in the nature of consciousness are completely withdrawn from every side. 132.
By those very waters of nectar consisting of the consciousness of the *śikha*, as they wash away the forms [of impurity],
the stains residing within consciousness— those belonging to *māyā* and the rest— attain complete cessation through Your will alone. 132.

O Blessed One, those whose power of action has been realized and whose vision of consciousness has long been graced by you through your favor do not become mere enjoyers of fruits within those various abodes of rebirth.
The atoms. 133.

The manifestation of power (*śākto vibhavaḥ*)— the majesty of the powers (*śaktīnām mahimā*)— is attained by those who have taken hold of it through devotion; these individual souls (*aṇavo jīvāḥ*), whose vision consists of consciousness (*saṃvinmayadṛṣṭi*) having been favored by you as you became gracious, [reside] in the heavens and other realms.
Furthermore, they do not become experiencers of the fruits of karma in the abodes of rebirth—that is, in the places of birth—because they are liberated. // 133 //
O Lord, while you have become a cloud of Dharma raining down abundant nectar within the cave of the heart,
the drop of the subtle atom (the individual soul), having been refined by the oyster-shell of manifest power, gradually attains [its true nature].
The nature of pure pearls. // 134 //

The Dharma is the nectar, the seed of liberation. When you have attained the state of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*) through the hearing of that [Dharma], the drop of the self (*ātmabindu*) attains the nature of a pure pearl;
as it is said: "From discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) comes the Cloud of Dharma samādhi."

After the attainment of the samādhi called Dharmameghā, one realizes the nature of purity and liberation. Within the cave-dweller—that which resides in the hollow of the heart—the power consisting of manifest gnosis itself is the mother-of-pearl; by that [power], there is the differentiation of living beings.

The subtle drop itself becomes refined and purified through the process of refinement (*saṃskṛti*), because it takes on that very form. When a cloud resting in a cave releases its water, the water-drop, through its excellence as a mother-of-pearl shell (*śukti*), attains the state of a pure pearl; so too does the nectar-like water. This is liberation (*mukti*).

That for which something is the purpose is *mauktika*. *Mukta* itself is *mauktika*. In one case, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to the rule *prāgvatīyaṣṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.82) meaning "having as its purpose"; in the other case, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied because [the word *muktā*] is included in the list beginning with *vinaya* (Pāṇini 5.4.34). 134.
When the wise man, having withdrawn his senses from other objects so that his inner self becomes steady and undisturbed, beholds you alone, he attains the vision of all things;
this is truly marvelous. 135.

He is one whose state is such that it has arisen through the internal instruments— the mind and so forth— which are undisturbed by the withdrawal of other objects such as sound, and which are steady, tranquil, and inward-turned in nature. His composure is characterized by such tranquility.
But it is a marvel that the Knower of All Objects, having discerned you alone, becomes a seer of things past, future, and so forth. 135.

O Lord, your power alone is capable of removing even the slightest trace of impure latent tendencies residing within the atoms of one's own self— tendencies that sever the bonds of existence— even as it brings about the manifestation of clarity, like the dawn.
Forgiveness. 136.
The Self alone, by virtue of its subtlety, is the atom; therefore, it is your own power that is capable of removing the latent impressions of the impurities of *māyā* which reside therein. 136.
Just as copper, having attained the state of gold through polishing, does not here again return to its state of copper, so too,
O Lord, the subtle principle (aṇutattva), once purified by Your will, does not fall back into such a state.
One's own latent predispositions. // 137 //

Just as copper, once it has attained the state of gold, never again becomes copper, so too the reality of the self (ātmatattva), having been rendered pure by Your will, is never again joined with the latent impressions of impurity.
And it has been said:
Just as copper rubbed with mercury does not again attain the state of being copper,
so too one who is united with Śiva does not again fall into the state of a bound soul (paśu).
Thus it goes; it proceeds. // 137 //
O Lord of the Gods, these three—Prakṛti, Puruṣa, and Praṇava—are situated like a well, a jar, and a rope.
Standing above them, firm and free from the manifold expansion of the senses, you wondrously draw them upward, O Aṇuman. 138.

Just as someone standing above draws up with a rope a jar that has fallen into a well, so should you [draw up] the Self, which has strayed from the reality of *prakṛti*, by means of the syllable *oṃ*. As it has been said:
"One should know *prakṛti* to be like a well, and the *puruṣa* likewise to be like a jar."

"Just as Śiva draws up even an atom by means of the syllable Oṃ, like a rope, so too he would lift out a jar or similar object fallen into a well; for he is equipped with instruments [for such tasks]. But that you do not do likewise—this is indeed strange. (138)
This transformation of the collection of phonemes, assuming both internal and external forms, exists in two ways;
it proceeds in direct order through the operation of the suffix *aṇ*, but it is set aside by you in reverse order.
This transformation of the *kalā*-tattva is of two kinds, consisting of internal and external forms.
In that regard, when Māyā transforms into the form of *kalā*, then Māyā itself— its body being veiled by the form of *kalā*— is called the transformation of *kalā*.
This is because it is both a *kalā* (limited power) and a transformation (*pariṇati*).

At that time, it possesses the status of being an internal factor (*antarāṅga*). However, when the *kalā* functions in the form of passion (*rāga*) and so forth, then, transforming into another form, it is called the "transformation of the *kalā*" (*kalā-pariṇati*) and is considered an external factor (*bahiraṅga*).

And this *anulominī* (ascending flow), proceeding by way of the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), is the "continuous activity" that binds the reality of the Self; the meaning is that it is the cause of dissolution (*saṃhāra*). However, by the reverse order (*prātilomya*), it is itself cast away by you alone, because all the principles (*tattva*) dissolve into you alone through their inversion.
The meaning is that, by means of the removal of passion and other afflictions, you alone are the cause of his liberation. // 139 //

O Lord, by taking refuge in you, the individual soul becomes free from the three states of existence, devoid of qualities and gender, established within the sky of the heart, and its sphere of activity is no longer the objects of the past or the future. (140)

Objects that have vanished or are yet to come into being—past, present, and future riches—the subtle Self (*ātman*) becomes the object of their existence by taking refuge in You; the meaning is that, having attained You alone, one perceives the entire collection of entities existing throughout the three periods of time. In this regard:

Because it follows the meaning of the suffix *bhāva*, the suffix *pratyaya* is like a superfluous goitre. It is that which does not possess the three states consisting of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; for it remains established by abiding in the fourth state (*turyapada*). It is devoid of qualities and marks because it is the Puruṣa.

It has attained the state of being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*) and the state of being without marks (*aliṅgatva*) because it is eternal; "mark" (*liṅga*) refers here to increase, decrease, and so forth. Others, however, hold that [the self] is devoid of marks and is not an object of inference because all means of valid cognition have ceased to apply to it.

Thus they say: because *tvad* is seen among the words beginning with *svar* (Pāṇini 1.1.37), it is an indeclinable expressing the sense of *yuṣmad*; it denotes the meaning of the genitive case. It should be treated as a separate word (*pṛthakpada*). However, a compound of *yuṣmad* is not possible, because there is a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*), just as in the case of "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*) when [the king] is aged. 140.
Just as these visual qualities, O Bhava, become manifest through contact with the rays of the sun,
so too do those of pure conduct become clarified through your proximity.
These depend upon the person. // 141 //
The qualities perceived by the eye are color-form, clarity, and extensiveness; the qualities of the Puruṣa consist of consciousness, sovereignty, virtue, and so forth. // 141 //

O Lord, that a person, though rendered incomplete by the total exhaustion of his powers, should nonetheless proceed along the most difficult path to liberation while remaining entirely without assistance— this is truly no wonder when You are well-pleased. 142.
Because of the complete exhaustion of desire and the like, he is without companion and solitary;

and even one who is deficient and powerless due to the loss of his capacity, being devoid of assistance, does not find it surprising that he traverses even a difficult path when the Lord is well-pleased. 142.
That stainless state which was indeed attained by those whose vows were sharpened by the practice of Amanaskayoga,
and who maintained an undisturbed stability within themselves— that, O Lord, is necessarily a consequence of Your grace. 143.

That state which is attained by those yogis whose vow is sharpened and keen— by whom that very stage of yoga is reached, which is "without mind" (amanaska), devoid of the mental activity consisting of conceptualization, taking the form of non-discernment (asamprajñāta), and which establishes itself as an unimpeded state within the stainless Self— is [the goal].
That [attainment] is inseparable from, and invariably concomitant with, your grace; the meaning is that it is obtained by that very [grace].
Through the grace produced by the dharma of manifest yoga, one becomes skilled in one's own nature, in the nature of others, and likewise in the nature of the Self.
Due to the transformation of the subtle mind, it extends consciousness toward other objects by your will.

Yoga itself is dharma; it is well-performed through your grace arising from that [dharma]. The transformation of the self, mind, and intellect—consisting of equanimity through the abandonment of external objects—is yoga.
Through this, yoga extends right knowledge not only within oneself but also throughout the continuums of others.
The meaning is that, according to your will, you render even insentient objects in other realms sentient, and likewise cause those that are conscious to become unconscious. // 144 //
That which is not described as the effect of egoism, which does not possess the quality of sound and is immutable,
wherein the host of stars does not shimmer, and wherein there is no movement— [that is the Supreme].
Somewhere from the wind. 145.
Beholding you stationed there in the sky— unobstructed, marked by the rainbow of the gods, and where no rows of clouds wander— the wise attained liberation.

146. (A pair of verses. Regarding the couplet beginning with "abhimāna": having beheld you in the sky—that is, within the space of the heart—yogins attained *apavarga*, meaning they reached liberation (*mokṣa*).

It is not said that the ether (ākāśa) has pride (abhimāna) as its effect; for external ether is produced from primordial nature (prakṛti), and from that comes the Great One (mahat), and from that the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). Thus, it is produced by the ego-sense through a traditional succession, and therefore this [ether] is distinct from it. 145–146.

A man who has attained the glory of self-realization through you, having fulfilled his purpose and abandoned the cycle of existence and non-existence, remains steadfast and discerns the five categories of reality; he attains a wondrous likeness to you, O Mistress. 147.
That man to whom you have bestowed and entrusted your own wealth attains equality with you, his lord; even a beast becomes a master. "Bhava" and "abhava" refer to manifestation and disappearance.
"In brief, the categories (padārtha) to be known in the unsurpassed Śaiva scripture are five: Vidhi, Kriyā, Kalā, Yoga, and Śiva.
Thus, even for a bound soul (paśu), the attainment of the state of being a Lord (pati) is truly wonderful. 147.
O Lord, just as the radiance of the sun, desiring to favor the circle of atoms, attains a state of stainlessness,
so too does your Śiva-śakti proceed in two forms, existing through the distinction of the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā).
It is twofold according to the distinction between the higher and the lower; that is to say, it is the bestower of liberation and the cause of enjoyment. //148//

O Lord, source of existence, who abides in both being and non-being, and whose majesty is manifested through the distinction of individuals who have entered the path—having attained a state of single-mindedness aided by spiritual power, the subtle [yogin] proceeds toward the range of the fourfold objects. 149.
O Source of Existence, O Destroyer! Having attained a single-mindedness toward you through your grace, his mind is assisted by knowledge and other virtues, becoming as subtle as an atom.

It attains the range of the four objects; that is to say, it proceeds toward the four objective domains consisting of knowledge of the dharmas, dispassion, and sovereignty. Existence and non-existence refer to saṃsāra and the absence of saṃsāra; by these two, the subtle self (aṇu) is grasped.
But the Supreme Lord is not like that; therefore, He is distinct from it.
Indeed, there is no separation between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*); here, neither does the function exist separately, nor is there one who possesses the function.
Others, who follow a non-contradictory path, declare that the very absence of that [mental activity] is the yoga of the mind. (150)
The nature of the pot is not distinct from the pot; thus, there is non-difference between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*).

Likewise, there is no separateness between the occurrence (*vṛtti*) and that which occurs (*vṛttimat*), because these two also possess the form of attribute and substratum. And it has been said: "There is no [separateness] between the occurrence and that which occurs..."

Difference [between the self and the mind] is ultimate. Thus, yoga is the cessation of the mere fluctuations of the mind; for when the fluctuations cease, that [mind] also ceases. Therefore, there is indeed the non-existence of the mind whose fluctuations, such as valid cognition and the rest, have been suppressed.
Others, who propound the meditative absorption on emptiness, declare that this is yoga; and it has been said: "One should contemplate non-existence until one attains identity with it. (150)

If this is indeed accepted, then surely everyone whose consciousness has ceased would clearly be liberated here without effort; yet, by your own wish, it is only that one who is stainless who possesses liberation. (151)

And this is incorrect; because if it were accepted in this way, it would follow that every yogi who possesses meditative absorption (*samādhi*) would have a mind entirely obstructed by the perception of non-existence. Yet such is not observed.
Rather, by your will alone, that yogi—liberated from the impurities of illusion and so forth—attains liberation. The meaning is that there is no cause for liberation other than your will. // 151 //
O Lord, those who were indeed made objects of Your grace through Your twofold self when You had entered the body of Vṛṣaga, they possess equality with You;
for their birth and destiny are distinct from those of the cave-dwellers (the Guhyakas) and other such beings, O Aṇu. 152.

Those atoms situated within Him, which— being of two kinds through the distinction between the higher and the lower— are made objects [of perception] by Your grace and are thus "without parts" (akalāḥ), meaning devoid of the principle of *kalā*, attain in due order equality with You; they are freed from the "darkness of the cave," that is, the impurity belonging to *māyā*, and are thus no longer subject to birth.
And they maintain that state. // 152 //

O All-pervading Lord, that sovereignty consisting of powers such as *aṇimā*—which exists among those dwelling on the earth and other realms up to the world of Brahmā (*parameṣṭhin*), which is unsurpassed by even the unconquered, and which resides within the gods—has manifested here, O Lord, solely through Your will; how wonderful! 153.
O Ajita, you are not overcome by anyone among the eightfold classes of divine beings— namely, the Brahmas, Prajāpatis, Indras, Pitṛs, Gandharvas, Nāgas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas.

The eightfold sovereignty, beginning with *aṇimā*, which resides successively in those established upon the earth and the rest— namely, in earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego— that has blossomed solely through Your will, extending from the Supreme Lord down to Brahmā.

The sovereignty of the Piśācas extends over the earth alone; that of the Rakṣasas, however, extends over both earth and water. Thus, by increasing one element at a time in sequence, it reaches the triad of all three elements belonging to Brahmā. // 153 //

O Lord of the Gods, because you have approached and established the majesty of the conscious self (cidātman) as the embodiment of all dharma, the entire circle of the world’s fetters functions without obstruction in all activities. 154.
By you, who have accepted that [the Self] consists of all existents, it has been established and demonstrated that the sovereign power whose nature is consciousness— that is,

its power of knowledge— exerts itself unimpededly in all actions and spreads forth without restraint, even while possessing a multitude of fetters such as passion and hatred; otherwise, [it could not do so].
Because that is not possible. // 154 //

Your power, endowed with the sovereignty of unimpeded self-majesty and firmly established as it is, never causes even your own atoms to waver in any of your worldly undertakings, whether directed toward superior or inferior beings. 155.

By your own majesty—through your omnipresence, sovereignty, and universal agency—your power is unimpeded; it is not obstructed anywhere. Because they are subtle, these very selves are the atoms within the liberated and experiencing selves, both higher and lower.
They do not waver from their duties, remaining steadfastly established therein. // 155 //
The entire circle of mantras consists of you; the Blessed One is accompanied by the host of gods and is of your own nature.
Alas! In this threefold world composed of the three qualities, there is indeed nothing that is not permeated by you. 156.
All mantras are identical with you; all gods are of the nature of mantras.
Therefore, within the threefold world consisting of Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar, there is nothing that could exist apart from you. And it has been said:
"All deities have the mantra as their essence; all mantras have Śiva as their essence.
Having realized that this [universe] has Śiva as its essence, one should contemplate only this.
Thus, they are imperishable, possessing the consciousness of the fruit which is free from all obstructions and consists of the entirety of the supreme and non-supreme.
The powers of you, the Lord, are like wish-fulfilling cows for the world, shedding an unrestrained stream of the water of immortality. 157.

The meaning is that those powers of yours, which are such that they fulfill all desires like wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus) throughout the worlds, are perfected with all riches; "immortality" refers to knowledge. // 157 //

Indeed, by Your will, those whose minds are unrestrained, led by the heroic Rudra Śatarudra and the lords of the Rudras, who are joined with the enjoyment of the qualities of Brahmā and others, enter the wondrous abode of Śiva. 158.
Led by Śatarudra and Vīrabhadra,
the one hundred and one Rudra leaders enter the state of Śiva solely through your will; so too does Brahmā, whose seat is the lotus.
Those whose nature it is to experience the qualities of those [beings] beginning from that point, such as being the initiators of creation and so forth—
the suffix *dhinuṇ* being applied here by the rule *saṃpṛca-ādi-sūtra*— they indeed become Vīrabhadra and appear ten by ten in each of the ten directions, and all of them above.
He who constantly remains experiencing the state of Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods is called Vīrabhadra, meaning "the Hero. 158.
Just as the eye, though its nature consists of complete vision and action, does not see when covered by cataracts and the like,
so too, O Lord, the atomic principle (aṇu-tattva) does not perceive anything when obstructed by impurities, except through Your grace. 159.
In both cases, it should be construed as: "that whose nature (bhāva) or essence (ātman) consists of the vision and action—that is, the activity of seeing—of the entire object. // 159 //

A person whose entire nature has been colored by your qualities, having quickly rubbed away the thick layer of impurity from his body, breaks through the firm cage of worldly existence as easily as a lotus-stalk.
The Blessed One [attained it] through reliance upon you. //160//
O Anaṅjana, that person who is free from the impurities of illusion and the like,
whose entire qualities are made radiant by your attributes such as knowledge,
shatters the cage of saṃsāra directly and swiftly, solely through taking refuge in you.
Ignorance, being overwhelmed by objects, lack of mastery, and lack of contemplation—these five are considered the human defects. 160.

Just as here, O Lord, the leaf of the banyan tree abandons its blueness and attains yellowness, so too, O Lord of Gods, the individual soul (aṇu), having cast off its state as a bound beast (paśu) and abiding in Your teaching, indeed attains the state of Śiva. 161.
"Chada" means a leaf; "fallen upon your teaching"—that is, upon your scripture—he has attained "śivatā," which is the state of having Śiva as his very nature. // 161 //
O Lord, when the darkness of bondage has been shattered by the rays of consciousness from Your heart, the skilled one,
having indeed realized the entire non-difference between the Kalā and the Puruṣa, [attains liberation].
One is liberated from the restrictive rules. // 162 //

When the darkness of delusion has been shattered by the rays of consciousness belonging to you within the mind, one who is skilled will necessarily attain liberation after discerning the distinction between the aggregate of phenomena and the true person.

O Lord of the Gods, just as a reflection is not perceived with clarity in a mirror that has become soiled, so too are you—though naturally pure—not clearly discerned when the mind is overwhelmed by a flood of impurities. Thus, through religious observance, may you become [clearly manifest].
Just as when a mirror has become soiled, a reflection is not perceived even due to its lack of clarity, so it is when your mind is defiled. 163.

O Haṃsa, you who possess a manifest form consisting of the entire circle of your own powers and offices, and who transcend the worlds of the senses, you utterly destroy the bonds of worldly existence for men who are enveloped in blinding darkness, even as they possess dense abundance.

O Haṃsa, O Supreme Self! You alone are superior—that is, preeminent—over the entire circle of your own powers (*śaktimaṇḍala*), which, while having the nature of a manifestation (*vivarta*) within all things, is yet distinct from them; for you are superior to the bodies, instruments, and worlds that constitute their inherent natures.

You destroy the great delusion that is the bond of existence for men, which in reality is the thick darkness of the self; you annihilate it. The genitive case is used according to the rule *jāsiniprahaṇa* (Pāṇini 2.3.56). *Nibirīsā* means dense or compact; [it is derived] by the addition of the suffixes *biḍac* and *birīsac* after the prefix *ni-* [according to the rule *nerbiḍajbirīsacau*]. 164.
O Lord of the Gods, having traversed the sixfold path of the flames of consciousness consisting of the eightfold manifestation of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*),
those established in the [proper] time enter your stainless state.
Of those wise ones whose minds are tranquil. // 165 //

However, those wise ones whose eightfold manifestation of consciousness— beginning with the *jyeṣṭha* and so forth— has proceeded either through the suddenness of fear or by means of their own creative intuition (*pratibhā*), transcend the path consisting of the principles (*tattva*) and other categories, and attain the stainless state.

Because they abide within your system (*samaya*). *Samaya* means established doctrine (*siddhānta*). And although [the powers] are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, as well as Raudrī, Kālī, Kālānusāriṇī, Kalā, Vikariṇī, Balapramathinī, Sarvabhūtapramathinī, and Manonmanī;
Thus, although there are nine consciousnesses beginning with Vāmā, nevertheless, Vāmā is excluded here because she is the cause of transmigratory existence. 165.

May he bestow the state of the nature of unobscured consciousness—eternal, inconceivable, immortal, and dwelling in the cave of the heart; whose form consists of his own innate powers manifested as distinct from one another through the stability of their primary, secondary, hidden, and supreme aspects. 166.
With the five verses beginning with "dadhataṃ," there is a *kulaka*: "The subtle self (*aṇv-ātman*), having entered into you, possesses a consciousness free from pleasure, pain, and so forth;
it is both primordial (*prākṛta*) and modified (*vaikṛta*), as well as derived from egoity (*āhaṃkārika*)."
It is remembered as being of the nature of sattva, rajas, and another, namely tamas.
"Consisting of both dharma and adharma—such is the eightfold bondage of the bound soul (paśu).
Thus, one becomes like Bhava himself, freed from the eightfold bondage consisting of the threads of the nature of fetters (pāśa).
This is indeed certain.

May they firmly maintain, as a constant rule, that state which is unobstructed, uninterrupted by space, time, and other such factors, whose nature is pure consciousness, unfathomable by logic, unknowable, and immortal— that is, liberation.
As for the designation of the Lord (*īśvara*) in this way, it is because he is the cause of that [liberation], just as one says "clarified butter is life."

"Abiding in the cave" means residing within the hollow of the heart. "Derivative" (gauṇa) refers to the embodied forms of Brahmā and others that arise from the qualities (guṇas), such as sattva and the rest. "Pertaining to the deep" (gāhanika) refers to that whose purpose is the profound [reality]. "Natural" (prākṛta) refers to the one known as Vigraheśvara, who holds authority over the principle of primordial nature (prakṛti-tattva).
The *gauha* is of the nature of *māyā*, because those [entities] such as Ekarudra and the others consist of *māyā*. Furthermore,

the *mālā* is entirely distinct from that, for it proceeds from the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) as the fundamental cause, since the leaders of the hosts (*gaṇanāyakas*) such as Megharudra and others have attained their status through that [cause].
He whose very form is power (*śakti*). And it has been said:

"Without a formal analysis (*vigraha*)—whether derivative (*gauṇa*), based on immersion (*gāhanika*), based on concealment (*gauha*), or primary (*maula*)—who else but you could exercise their respective authority as a distinct manifestation of power?"
Thus [ends the section]. 166.

The entire [reality], devoid of parts, free from the cycle of rebirth, unassailed by calamity, yet appearing as if situated amidst external disturbances; standing beyond the six-limbed path, transcending all, peaceful, faultless, and supremely auspicious.

It is both *sakala* (with parts) as the soul of the universe, and *akala* (without parts), being devoid of the principle of *kalā*; thus there is a contradiction in how that which is *sakala* can be *akala*. It is "without movement" (*plavena gatyā rahitam*) because it is omnipresent.
It is "undisturbed" (*nirupaplava*), meaning it is not corrupted by passion and other afflictions; for this very reason, it stands outside of all disturbances.

His state is situated outside of saṃsāra; he stands above the path (adhvan) consisting of the six categories, such as the principles (tattva) and so forth, having transcended it. For this very reason, he is "transcended" (vyativṛtta), beyond the universe, peaceful, and entirely incomparable.
"Anagham" means faultless; "param" means supreme; "śivam" means auspicious. // 167 //
He transcends the two types of manifestation, possesses clearly manifest attributes such as immeasurability, and has reached a state beyond description;
He is the primordial God, both atomic and non-atomic, the all-pervasive Lord whose faces, heads, hands, feet, and eyes are everywhere.
*Pratibhā* is a cognition characterized by a novel manifestation; it is of two kinds, innate and acquired.

[The object] transcends that [cognition], meaning it is beyond its scope. Precisely for that reason, it is such that it lacks connection with properties such as being an object of knowledge (*meyatva*) or being expressible (*nirdeśyatva*).

For this very reason, it is indefinable and indescribable; it is subtle (*aṇu*) because its nature is the Self, and it is non-subtle (*anaṇu*) or gross because it consists of the universe. Here too, as before, there is a contradiction.
It is that whose heads and other limbs extend everywhere and are directed in all directions. And thus:
He who is recited as the all-seeing, indeed as the one whose face is on every side, whose hands are on every side, and whose feet are on every side. 168.
He has assumed a form consisting of five stable faces, illuminated by his own limbs which remain undisturbed;
he is the planet that seizes the body, having reached a state of profound selfhood that is devoid of any apprehension of existence and transcends the scope of all means of valid cognition.

He is one whose assumption of a body is illuminated by his own limbs, such as the hands and so forth, which remain in a single form through an undisturbed state; or by the heart and other centers, which consist of the nature of omniscience; and he possesses five faces, such as Sadyojāta and the others, which are composed of jewels.

Because that state which transcends the objects of all means of valid cognition, such as direct perception and the rest, is for that reason devoid of conceptual apprehension and thus not an object of inference; and for this very reason, it is profound.
O Śaṅkara, having attained you, the imperishable one, with a consciousness freed from pleasure, pain, and delusion,
and having transcended the eightfold bonds consisting of the threads [of the gunas], O Blessed One, he clearly becomes an atom (aṇu) like you. 170.
At the time of universal dissolution, your circular face with its copper-red palate, opened wide by your singular thirst to swallow the world,
attains a beauty like the shimmering orb of the sun, rosy with the hue of a clinging lotus.
The locus of the sacrificial fee. 171.
The southern site is that which is situated in the southern part and is named Aghora. 171–172.
Adorned by the rays of jewels from the circle of hoods flashing upon the lordly serpents that form his broad topknot,
he who rests upon your head bestows prosperity upon you, like the young moon bearing the glow of twilight.
Your forehead-eye shines forth, suffused by the orb of rays from the moon that serves as your crest-ornament;
it has taken its seat there, as if assuming a splendor fashioned from the remnants of the ashes of Smara, by means of its odd-numbered radiance.
The one with uneven rays is the seven-rayed one. 173.

In ancient times, with an arrow whose brilliance was unshaken as it was forged by blazing fire, which dried up the waters of the celestial river with its broad shaft, you destroyed the three cities; and later, with your upward-rolling eye, you destroyed the god of love.

He whose splendor is joined with that of Acyuta Viṣṇu—because [the mountain] was made into the body of Hari during the burning of the cities; elsewhere, "acyutāḥ" means firm, and "hetayaḥ" means flames—you have burnt it. (174–175)

O Lord, this formidable mass of matted hair of yours, entwined with newly sloughed black serpents, shines forth tawny like a circle of smoke from the fire blazing in the eye on your forehead, which is agitated by its constant flickering. 175.
Having assumed a body composed of black night, O Daughter of the Mountain, it does not leave you for even a moment,
under the guise of a mass of luster ashen-grey with the manifest Kālakūṭa poison.
The circle of the broad neck. 176.
"Even for a moment" means even for a single instant. // 176 //
O Lord, when you were burning the cities, you caused the orb of the moon to become the wheels for Kṣitiratha;
its spot was obscured, its dark interior luster vanished, and it appeared as if its central cavity had burst open.
It is observed. 177.
The earth itself was the chariot; its central aperture was the luster of Malina’s belly, which had been marked by the deer that had been bound to it. 177–178.
O Lord of the Gods, throughout the many cycles of the world’s dissolution that have passed away,
the stainless circle of planets you have accumulated serves as a rosary of crystal beads for you.

O Lord, the young moon dances before you as if out of haste to receive your instruction, appearing like a cloud heavy with water due to its neck being adorned with the manifest mass of kālakūṭa poison.
Candrakī is a peacock. 179.
O Lord Śaṅkara, by performing dances throughout all the nights with detailed procedures of hand gestures (*karaṇa*) and bodily movements (*aṅgahāra*),
you, O All-pervading One, having attained this world of the moving and the unmoving, enact a likeness of yourself.
Of those who stand still. // 180 //

By dancing during the nights, you are performing an imitation of yourself alone, since there exists no other object to be imitated apart from yourself. The instruments are the *talapuṣpapuṭa* and others; the *aṅgahāras* are the *sthirahasta* and other such gestures. // 180 //

You, who have established the lineage of those practicing the path and have taken firm residence in the abode of your father along with your mother— O Blessed One, you are clearly celebrated as the beginningless King and as the Ancient Puruṣa.
He who has taken up his lineage from Mount Kailāsa as his support, for whom the cremation ground is the father’s home, and whose mothers are the deities such as Vārāhī and others—
he who possesses the lineage beginning with the creation of the world dwells in the father’s house together with his mother.
And here, the contradiction is implied as to how the King can be both beginningless and ancient.

O Hara, even by the hosts of gods and demons who bow down— themselves rendered humble by being reflected in the surface of the mirrors that are the nails of your lotus-feet— you attain greatness that surpasses all others. 182.

By those who have made themselves light through the power of prostration, with their bodies contracted, "greatness" means excellence. There is a contradiction here: how can those who, being reflected in the surface of the nails, are of a light form, be "great"—that is, bulky? By this very [contradiction]...
This same method of interpretation should also be applied to what follows. 182.

The multitude of beings bows down to the pair of your lotus feet— the refuge of the world including both gods and asuras— and even while thus prostrate, they do not sink downward anywhere, just as a flame of fire does not descend to the ground. 183.
Āśuśukṣaṇi is the burner. // 183 //

Salutations to You, the Supreme Self, whose nature transcends the sphere of thought, sound, and conceptualization, and who manifests as the forms of earth, water, wind, fire, sun, sky, moon, and the sacrificer. 184.

That whose nature is preeminent, insofar as it has not entered the state of being an object for conceptual cognition— that is, for the cognition of a mother— and for verbal conceptualizations, because it is beyond their range;
[this applies] even without the use of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).
Its meaning is understood [by implication], just as in the rule "the dual and singular endings are used for two and one" (Pāṇini 1.4.22). // 184 //
O Lord, even the conceptual constructions of the wise, which fall within the range of intellect and speech, do not find a stable footing in You here;
therefore, I desist from this undertaking, though I am thirsty to utter even a few words regarding Your infinitesimal qualities.

Therefore, even for Sumati, conceptual constructions—known as mental fabrications (*vikalpa*)—which fall within the range of the word "intellect" (*mati*) and are caused by the resonance of knowledge, find no footing in you; nor can you be grasped even by them.
Thus, though I am thirsty for even a mere fragment of your virtues through these well-spoken words, [I remain unable to describe them].
One desists from that exertion. // 185 //

By what cause does the grace of the Preceptor of the Gods manifest toward you even when you are situated at an extreme distance, yet fail to manifest toward you even when you are close at hand? And by what cause does its opposite occur?

By whose power you are seen even when far away because you reside in the heart, yet are not perceived even when nearby; by what cause does that favor of yours manifest, and its opposite, the lack of favor? The meaning is: "Tell me the reason for these two. (186)
Or rather, let this marvelous feat of yours remain for now— you whose consciousness is devoid of resentment;
listen to that which you should keep in mind.
We have taken refuge in you, the unborn and undecaying one. 187.
Even for those yogis who possess unobstructed knowledge and whose consciousness is empty of aversion, your conduct remains a source of wonder. 187.

Once, while he was staying happily on the Himalayas, his face graced by the playful jests of her smiling countenance, the Daughter of the Mountain approached him secretly from behind; as he had closed his eyes, she covered them with her lotus-like hands. (188)
We have heard—that is, we have learned—from tradition that a person was born from the Blessed One who was staying on Himācala. 188–191.
O Lord, we have heard that in the past, from the Primordial Puruṣa, there suddenly arose a Puruṣa deprived of his eyes,
like the seed of the mass of darkness swelling forth at the onset of the night of the Time of Destruction.
189. (A pair of verses) Then,
by that name "Andhaka," which was clearly meaningful and renowned throughout the three worlds, he [was known].
At this very time, you granted a boon to the son of Diti, who was performing difficult austerities for the sake of a son.
Then, having attained prosperity in his palace, cherished by the caresses of Manorama’s embrace,
he began to practice unrestrained and most difficult austerity, intent upon destroying the blinding darkness [of ignorance].
Having obtained eyes from the Self-Existent One through penance accumulated over a long time,
he attained the unshakable sovereignty over the worlds— a realm where gods and demons were stripped of their mutual enmity.
*Pratimalla* means a rival combatant; that is to say, one who fights as an equal. // 192 //
Having reached its station upon the chest of Viṣṇu, the discus also— dispelling the mass of darkness with its rays—
proceeded like the shimmering orb of the sun upon the peak of the western mountain.
The state of being devoid of majesty. // 193 //
*Pratāpa* is the splendor of valor and intense heat. // 193 //
In battles, the spray of sweat-drops from the heat of Hari’s indignation— conquered by his intense [exertion]—
wiped the face of [his opponent], whose fierce knitting of the eyebrows was [thus cleared].
The tears, darkened by the shadow [of grief], are falling incessantly.
Analysis is dissection. // 194 //
Thus, O Lord, he whose glorious command— by which the Fortune of the World-Guardians was made to pay tribute— crowns their heads,
has taken us captive as prisoners in the forest at the edge of his camp.
Because of the cause of bondage existing simultaneously with constant connection. // 195 //

He whose glorious command— its crest occupied by the Fortune (Lakṣmī) of Indra and the other gods who have been made tributaries and established as payers of tribute— is carried out upon their heads; [he is] Bandī.
A woman taken by force; *ketana* means a house. // 195 //
Therefore, perform now that which is appropriate for this moment; for here is Hari himself, accompanied by the world-protectors,
following you so that you may clearly desire to cross even the ocean of saṃsāra.
O sinless one, you are a raft; how much more so for one suffering from the pain of distress? 196.
"Prāptakālam" means having reached the proper time; that is to say, it is opportune. "Anvak" means afterwards. "Plava" means a raft or a means of crossing. // 196 //
When he had thus uttered his speech and remained silent with face turned downward,
there immediately ensued the playful onset of anger among the Gaṇapas, who had previously arrived at that place.
By the clapping of her palms, the gems on her finger-rings were crushed. 197.
*Arvāgdha-apavṛtti* means returning from nearby; *velā* refers to the shore or time; *ūrmikā* means a ring for the finger.
